trans-unit.source: Peripateticware began as a white paper written inside McGraw-Hill Education. It argued that GPS-enabled mobile devices would transform learning — that students walking through real places, guided by structured inquiry, could learn in a way textbooks never allowed.
trans-unit.target: Peripateticware הפך את העיצוב כספר בסבילה של מחבר מגרפי. זה נאמר בספר הביאופיה שלו, שהוא מתפרסם ב-McGraw-Hill Education. זה החל מכך שהתגובות GPS-enabled mobile devices (התקנות מובילות על טלפון) תוסף את המודרניזם החינם בתוך המודרניזם המושכים בספרים, ואף על פי כן שהאונלין יוכל ללמד בגון שהטקנות הספרים שלא היו כותבות זאת.

trans-unit.source: The paper named one problem it couldn't solve: assessment. How do you evaluate learning that happens in a creek bed, or at a cathedral arch, or in a city park? In 2026, AI finally gave us the answer.
trans-unit.target: השורש נמצא בכתב הדיסקס עהמבז לפתרון: הגרמה. כאשר אנחנו מעריכים ה学习 שקיבוצה בקדר המסגרים, או בפרוז הקathedralה או בחוף העיר? ב 2026, AI שלוח נוסף את העמוד.

trans-unit.source: The assessment problem turned out to have two parts. The first was capturing evidence — what did the student actually observe, and can you prove it? The second was evaluating it — did their thinking deepen, or did they just describe what they saw?

trans-unit.source: The first part was solved by smartphones. What remained was the second part: structured inquiry that didn't just document experience but deepened it.

trans-unit.source: That's where Peri comes in. Peri is Peripateticware's AI guide — named, like the software, after the Aristotelian method. Peri doesn't answer questions. It asks them. Peri takes a student's observation and asks the next right question. When the student gets it right, Peri tests the implication. When the student is vague, Peri asks for evidence.
